claim: CRM1 mediates nuclear export of hundreds of proteins through recognition of their nuclear export signals (NESs).
source: The exportin CRM1 (Chromosome Region Maintenance 1 protein; also known as exportin 1 or XPO1) is the most prominent nuclear export receptor in the cell. CRM1 maintains the cellular localization of hundreds of diverse-functioning protein cargos, including many tumor suppressor, cell cycle proteins, and viral proteins (Fornerod et al., 1997; Fukuda et al., 1997; Ossareh-Nazari et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Fornerod et al., 1997; Fukuda et al., 1997; Ossareh-Nazari et al., 1997)

claim: CRM1 is a promising cancer drug target.
source: CRM1 is also a promising cancer drug target, and a small molecule inhibitor of CRM1 named Selinexor is currently in more than 40 clinical trials for a variety of cancers (clinicaltrials.gov) (Lapalombella et al., 2012; Etchin et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013; Fung and Chook, 2014; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and clinical trial data (Lapalombella et al., 2012; Etchin et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013; Fung and Chook, 2014; Xu et al., 2015)

claim: Selinexor is a small molecule inhibitor of CRM1 currently in more than 40 clinical trials for a variety of cancers.
source: CRM1 is also a promising cancer drug target, and a small molecule inhibitor of CRM1 named Selinexor is currently in more than 40 clinical trials for a variety of cancers (clinicaltrials.gov) (Lapalombella et al., 2012; Etchin et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013; Fung and Chook, 2014; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and clinical trial data (Lapalombella et al., 2012; Etchin et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013; Fung and Chook, 2014; Xu et al., 2015)

claim: NESs are 8–15 residue long sequences in proteins.
source: CRM1 recognizes its protein cargos through 8–15 residue long nuclear export signals (NESs) in the proteins (la Cour et al., 2004; Kosugi et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (la Cour et al., 2004; Kosugi et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2010)

claim: NES sequences are highly diverse.
source: NES sequences are highly diverse, and the peptides bind CRM1 with a large affinity range, with dissociation constants (KDs) ranging from low nanomolar to tens of micromolar (Kutay and Guttinger, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Kutay and Guttinger, 2005)

claim: NES peptides bind CRM1 with dissociation constants (KDs) ranging from low nanomolar to tens of micromolar.
source: NES sequences are highly diverse, and the peptides bind CRM1 with a large affinity range, with dissociation constants (KDs) ranging from low nanomolar to tens of micromolar (Kutay and Guttinger, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Kutay and Guttinger, 2005)

claim: NESs are best described by a set of six consensus sequences that differ in the spacings between four key hydrophobic residues Φ1, Φ2, Φ3, and Φ4.
source: Sequence, peptide-library, and bioinformatic analyses have found that NESs are best described by a set of six consensus sequences, which differ in the spacings between four key hydrophobic residues Φ1, Φ2, Φ3, and Φ4 (Figure 1A) (la Cour et al., 2004; Kosugi et al., 2008; Xu, Farmer et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (la Cour et al., 2004; Kosugi et al., 2008; Xu, Farmer et al., 2012a) and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Structures are available for only three different NESs bound to CRM1: from PKI, Snurportin-1, and HIV1-Rev protein.
source: Structures are available for only three different NESs, from the cargos protein kinase A inhibitor (PKI), Snurportin-1 (SNUPN), and the HIV1-Rev protein, bound to CRM1.
evidence: Statement about the state of structural knowledge at the time of writing

claim: NESs bind in a hydrophobic groove located on the outer/convex surface of the ring-shaped CRM1.
source: The NESs bind in a hydrophobic groove, which is located on the outer/convex surface of the ring-shaped CRM1 (Dong et al., 2009; Monecke et al., 2009; Güttler et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Dong et al., 2009; Monecke et al., 2009; Güttler et al., 2010)

claim: NESs use almost exclusively their side chains, especially their hydrophobic Φ side chains, to bind CRM1.
source: The NESs use almost exclusively their side chains, especially their hydrophobic Φ side chains, to bind CRM1.
evidence: Based on structural observations from previous studies

claim: The NES-binding groove of CRM1 consists of 5 hydrophobic pockets P0–P4.
source: The NES-binding groove of CRM1, which is wide at one end and narrow at the other end, consists of 5 hydrophobic pockets P0–P4 and is virtually identical in all CRM1-NES structures (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and based on structural observations

claim: The NES-binding groove of CRM1 is wide at one end and narrow at the other end.
source: The NES-binding groove of CRM1, which is wide at one end and narrow at the other end, consists of 5 hydrophobic pockets P0–P4 and is virtually identical in all CRM1-NES structures (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and based on structural observations

claim: The NES-binding groove of CRM1 is virtually identical in all CRM1-NES structures.
source: The NES-binding groove of CRM1, which is wide at one end and narrow at the other end, consists of 5 hydrophobic pockets P0–P4 and is virtually identical in all CRM1-NES structures (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on comparison of multiple CRM1-NES structures

claim: PKINES and SNUPNNES share a similar structure when bound to CRM1: an N-terminal 3-turn α-helix followed by a short C-terminal β-strand-like extension.
source: NESs from PKI and SNUPN (PKINES and SNUPNNES) share a similar structure when bound to CRM1—an N-terminal 3-turn α-helix followed by a short C-terminal β-strand-like extension (Figure 1B) (Dong et al., 2009; Monecke et al., 2009; Güttler et al., 2010; Koyama et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Dong et al., 2009; Monecke et al., 2009; Güttler et al., 2010; Koyama et al., 2014) and shown in Figure 1B

claim: The NES helix binds the wide part of the CRM1 groove, while the β-strand binds the narrow end of the groove.
source: The NES helix binds the wide part of the CRM1 groove, while the β-strand binds the narrow end of the groove.
evidence: Based on structural observations from previous studies

claim: The RevNES peptide binds the CRM1 groove in a different manner by adopting an entirely extended conformation.
source: The RevNES peptide binds the CRM1 groove in a different manner by adopting an entirely extended conformation (Güttler et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Güttler et al., 2010)

claim: All three previously studied NES peptides (PKI, SNUPN, Rev) bind in the same direction, with their N-termini at the wide part of the groove.
source: All three NES peptides bind in the same direction, with their N-termini at the wide part of the groove.
evidence: Based on structural observations from previous studies

claim: The vastly different conformations of the extended RevNES compared to the helix-strand PKINES and SNUPNNES suggest that CRM1 may recognize divergent signal sequences in part by binding different peptide structures.
source: The vastly different conformations of the extended RevNES compared to the helix-strand PKINES and SNUPNNES suggest that CRM1 may recognize divergent signal sequences in part by binding different peptide structures.
evidence: Inference based on structural observations

claim: The class 3 NES consensus of Φ1X(2,3)Φ2X(2,3)Φ3X2Φ4 with two intervening residues between Φ3 and Φ4 suggests a single long NES helix.
source: For example, the class 3 NES consensus of Φ1X(2,3)Φ2X(2,3)Φ3X2Φ4 with two intervening residues between Φ3 and Φ4 suggests a single long NES helix.
evidence: Inference based on sequence pattern and structural constraints

claim: Class 3 NES sequences are as prevalent as NESs of classes 1b, 1c, 1d, and 2 in current NES databases.
source: In current NES databases, class 3 NES sequences are as prevalent as NESs of classes 1b, 1c, 1d, and 2, but information of how they are able to bind CRM1 is missing (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Xu et al., 2015)

claim: Crystallization of CRM1-Ran-NES peptide complexes has generally not been successful, possibly due to conformational flexibility and low affinities for the NESs.
source: Crystallization of CRM1-Ran-NES peptide complexes has generally not been successful, possibly due to conformational flexibility and low affinities for the NESs (Kutay and Guttinger, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Kutay and Guttinger, 2005) and speculation about reasons

claim: The ternary complex of Saccharomyces cerevisiae CRM1 with RanGTP and RanBP1 reliably yields crystals that diffract to high resolution.
source: On the other hand, the ternary complex of Saccharomyces cerevisiae CRM1 (ScCRM1) with RanGTP (human or yeast RanGTP, Gsp1p) and RanBP1 (Yrb1p) reliably yields crystals that diffract to high resolution and has been used to determine structures of several CRM1-inhibitor complexes (Koyama and Matsuura, 2010; Lapalombella et al., 2012; Etchin et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013; Haines et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Koyama and Matsuura, 2010; Lapalombella et al., 2012; Etchin et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013; Haines et al., 2015)

claim: RanBP1 binding normally stimulates NES release by closing the NES-binding groove of ScCRM1.
source: RanBP1 binding normally stimulates NES release by closing the NES-binding groove of ScCRM1 (Koyama and Matsuura, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Koyama and Matsuura, 2010)

claim: Mutation of the H9 loop of CRM1 (Val441Asp) stabilizes the open CRM1 groove.
source: Koyama and Matsuura showed that mutation of the H9 loop of CRM1, which packs against the back of a closed NES groove, stabilizes the open CRM1 groove (Koyama and Matsuura, 2010). Thus, we mutated the H9 loop (Val441Asp) to detach it from the back of the NES groove and to open the groove even when CRM1 is complexed with Ran and RanBP1.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Koyama and Matsuura, 2010)

claim: The CRM1* construct binds NES peptides in the presence of RanGTP and RanBP1.
source: The resulting CRM1* construct, with ScCRM1 residues 1–1058, Δ377–413, V441D and groove residues 537DLTVK541 mutated to GLCEQ (to mimic human CRM1, see methods), binds NES peptides in the presence of RanGTP and RanBP1.
evidence: Experimental observation from this study

claim: Crystal structures of CRM1*-RanGppNHp-RanBP1-hRio2NES and CRM1*-RanGppNHp-RanBP1-CPEB4NES complexes were determined to 2.3 Å and 2.1 Å resolution, respectively.
source: We generated quaternary CRM1*-RanGppNHp-RanBP1-NES complexes with two class 3 NES peptides, the hRio2NES (389RSFEMTEFNQALEEI403) and the CPEB4NES (379RTFDMHSLESSLIDI393; predicted Φ1–Φ4 positions are underlined) and determined their structures to 2.3 Å and 2.1 Å resolution (Figure 1C,D; crystallographic statistics in Table 1).
evidence: Experimental data from this study shown in Figure 1C,D and Table 1

claim: hRio2NES residues 391–403 and CPEB4NES residues 379–393 were modeled in the respective structures.
source: hRio2NES residues 391–403 and CPEB4NES residues 379–393 were modeled in the respective structures.
evidence: Experimental data from this study

claim: hRio2NES and CPEB4NES bind the CRM1 groove in the opposite or minus direction compared to previous NES structures.
source: The CRM1-bound hRio2NES and CPEB4NES structures unexpectedly revealed that both NESs bound the CRM1 groove in opposite orientation (termed the minus direction) compared to previous NES structures (PKINES, SNUPNNES, and RevNES bind in the plus direction) (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: Experimental data from this study shown in Figure 1B,D

claim: The NES groove of CRM1 is nearly invariant when bound to plus or minus NESs.
source: The NES groove of CRM1 is nearly invariant when bound to plus or minus NESs (Cα rmsds 0.3–0.5 Å; all atom rmsds 1.0–1.3 Å, for CRM1 residues 521–605 in all available CRM1-NES structures [Dong et al., 2009; Monecke et al., 2009; Güttler et al., 2010]).
evidence: Experimental data from this study compared with published structures (Dong et al., 2009; Monecke et al., 2009; Güttler et al., 2010)

claim: Local structures of the hRio2NES and CPEB4NES are similar to those of the PKINES and SNUPNNES.
source: Although the polypeptide directions are reversed, local structures of the hRio2NES and CPEB4NES are similar to those of the PKINES and SNUPNNES.
evidence: Experimental data from this study

claim: All four NES peptides (hRio2, CPEB4, PKI, SNUPN) are combinations of 3-turn α-helices and 2-residue β-strand-like extensions.
source: All four NES peptides are combinations of 3-turn α-helices and 2-residue β-strand-like extensions.
evidence: Experimental data from this study

claim: In minus NESs, helices are at the C-termini of the peptides and their strands at the N-termini.
source: Helices of the minus NESs are now at the C-termini of the peptides and their strands at the N-termini (Figure 1D).
evidence: Experimental data from this study shown in Figure 1D

claim: Both plus and minus NES helices bind the same part of the CRM1 groove, with hydrophobic residues from one helix face occupying hydrophobic pockets P0–P3 of CRM1.
source: Both plus and minus NES helices bind the same part of the CRM1 groove, with hydrophobic residues from one helix face occupying hydrophobic pockets P0–P3 of CRM1 (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: Experimental data from this study shown in Figure 1B,D

claim: The two minus NESs match the consensus pattern Φ1XΦ2XXXΦ3XXΦ4XXΦ5, which is the reverse of the class 1a pattern.
source: The structures show that the two minus NESs clearly match the consensus pattern Φ1XΦ2XXXΦ3XXΦ4XXΦ5, which is the reverse of the class 1a pattern, Φ0XXΦ1XXΦ2XXXΦ3XΦ4.
evidence: Experimental data from this study

claim: The five hydrophobic residues of the hRio2NES and CPEB4NES bind the same P0–P4 pockets as the plus NESs, but in reverse order, with Φ1 in P4 and Φ5 in P0.
source: The five hydrophobic residues of the hRio2NES and CPEB4NES, designated Φ1–Φ5, bind the same P0–P4 pockets as the plus NESs, but in reverse order, with Φ1 in P4 and Φ5 in P0 (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: Experimental data from this study shown in Figure 1B,D

claim: hRio2NES and CPEB4NES are not class 3 NESs in the traditional sense, as the four previously designated Φ residues do not occupy the P1–P4 hydrophobic pockets as predicted.
source: The hRio2NES and CPEB4NES are in fact not class 3 NESs in the traditional sense, as the four previously designated Φ residues in hRio2NES (389RSFEMTEFNQALEEI403) and the CPEB4NES (379RTFDMHSLESSLIDI393; predicted Φ1–Φ4 positions are underlined) do not occupy the P1–P4 hydrophobic pockets as predicted.
evidence: Experimental data from this study

claim: Comparison of plus and minus NESs showed translational offsets of the helices along their axes.
source: Comparison of plus and minus NESs showed translational offsets of the helices along their axes (Figure 2).
evidence: Experimental data from this study shown in Figure 2

claim: Cαs of minus NESs are shifted 1.3–3.5 Å from equivalent Cαs in the plus NESs, with the largest shifts observed for residues that occupy the P0 and P1 CRM1 pockets.
source: Cαs of minus NESs are shifted 1.3–3.5 Å from equivalent Cαs in the plus NESs, with the largest shifts observed for residues that occupy the P0 and P1 CRM1 pockets.
evidence: Experimental data from this study

claim: Medium-sized hydrophobic side chains such as isoleucine and leucine are preferred at Φ4 and Φ5 positions of hRio2NES for CRM1 interaction.
source: Results of in vitro pull-down assays using immobilized GST-hRio2NES mutants, purified human CRM1, and yeast RanGTP show that medium-sized hydrophobic side chains such as isoleucine and leucine are preferred at Φ4 and Φ5 for CRM1 interaction.
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 3A

claim: Medium and larger hydrophobic side chains such as isoleucine, leucine, and methionine are preferred at Φ3 position of hRio2NES for binding CRM1.
source: Medium and larger hydrophobic side chains such as isoleucine, leucine, and methionine are preferred at Φ3 for binding CRM1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 3A

claim: Large hydrophobic side chains such as leucine, methionine, phenylalanine, and tryptophan are preferred in both Φ1 and Φ2 positions of hRio2NES.
source: Mutagenesis of the Φ1 and Φ2 positions of hRio2NES and pull-down assays with CRM1 and Ran show that large hydrophobic side chains such as leucine, methionine, phenylalanine, and tryptophan are preferred in both positions (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 3B

claim: Smaller hydrophobic side chains like alanine, valine, and isoleucine in Φ1 and Φ2 positions of hRio2NES are disfavored as the mutants do not bind CRM1 efficiently.
source: Smaller hydrophobic side chains like alanine, valine, and isoleucine in these positions are disfavored as the mutants do not bind CRM1 efficiently (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 3B

claim: The preference for large hydrophobic side chains in Φ1 and Φ2 positions is consistent with the need for side chains in the extended portions of the minus NESs to reach farther into their CRM1-binding sites.
source: The preference for large hydrophobic side chains is consistent with the need for side chains in the extended portions of the minus NESs to reach farther into their CRM1-binding sites.
evidence: Inference based on structural observations and mutagenesis data

claim: Large aromatic residues phenylalanine and tryptophan are disfavored in equivalent Φ3 and Φ4 positions in the plus direction PKINES.
source: In contrast, the large aromatic residues phenylalanine and tryptophan are disfavored in equivalent Φ3 and Φ4 positions in the plus direction PKINES (Güttler et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Güttler et al., 2010)

claim: Placement of the strand-like ΦXΦ motif at the N-terminus of an NES generates a signal peptide that binds CRM1 in the minus direction.
source: Structural and mutagenesis data to compare plus and minus NESs suggest that placement of the strand-like ΦXΦ motif at the N-terminus of an NES generates a signal peptide that binds CRM1 in the minus direction, whereas a C-terminal ΦXΦ results in a plus direction NES.
evidence: Inference based on structural and mutagenesis data from this study

claim: A C-terminal ΦXΦ motif results in a plus direction NES.
source: Structural and mutagenesis data to compare plus and minus NESs suggest that placement of the strand-like ΦXΦ motif at the N-terminus of an NES generates a signal peptide that binds CRM1 in the minus direction, whereas a C-terminal ΦXΦ results in a plus direction NES.
evidence: Inference based on structural and mutagenesis data from this study

claim: Wild-type MBP-hRio2NES binds CRM1 with a KD of 2200 nM [1600,2900].
source: Wild-type NESs MBP-hRio2NES and MBP-CPEB4NES bind CRM1 with KDs of 2200 nM [1600,2900] and 590 nM [400,840], respectively (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental data from competition differential bleaching experiments shown in Figure 4B

claim: Wild-type MBP-CPEB4NES binds CRM1 with a KD of 590 nM [400,840].
source: Wild-type NESs MBP-hRio2NES and MBP-CPEB4NES bind CRM1 with KDs of 2200 nM [1600,2900] and 590 nM [400,840], respectively (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental data from competition differential bleaching experiments shown in Figure 4B

claim: MBP-hRio2NES-R binds CRM1 with a KD of 2400 nM [2100,2800].
source: When NES sequences are reversed, MBP-hRio2NES-R and MBP-CPEB4NES-R still bind CRM1 with similar affinities, KDs of 2400 nM [2100,2800] and 780 nM [610,980], respectively (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Experimental data from competition differential bleaching experiments shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: MBP-CPEB4NES-R binds CRM1 with a KD of 780 nM [610,980].
source: When NES sequences are reversed, MBP-hRio2NES-R and MBP-CPEB4NES-R still bind CRM1 with similar affinities, KDs of 2400 nM [2100,2800] and 780 nM [610,980], respectively (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Experimental data from competition differential bleaching experiments shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: All tested NES peptides (hRio2NES, CPEB4NES, hRio2NES-R, CPEB4NES-R) direct nuclear export in a Leptomycin B sensitive manner in HeLa cells.
source: All of the NES peptides were also cloned into EYFP-NLS-NES fusions and tested for nuclear export activity in HeLa cells. They were all found to direct nuclear export in a Leptomycin B sensitive manner, suggesting that the reverse peptides function as active NESs in cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Experimental data from cellular localization assays shown in Figure 4C

claim: Crystal structures of CRM1-bound hRio2NES-R and CPEB4NES-R peptides were solved at 2.3 Å and 2.9 Å resolution, respectively.
source: Crystal structures of CRM1-bound hRio2NES-R and CPEB4NES-R peptides were solved at 2.3 Å and 2.9 Å resolution, respectively (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: Experimental data from this study shown in Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Table 1

claim: hRio2NES-R and CPEB4NES-R peptides bind in the plus direction, opposite that of their wild-type counterparts.
source: These structures show the peptides binding in the plus direction, that is, opposite that of their wild-type counterparts (Figure 5A).
evidence: Experimental data from this study shown in Figure 5A

claim: The CRM1 grooves in the hRio2NES-R and CPEB4NES-R complexes are almost identical to those in the wild-type hRio2NES and CPEB4NES complexes.
source: The CRM1 grooves in the hRio2NES-R and CPEB4NES-R complexes are almost identical to those in the wild-type hRio2NES and CPEB4NES complexes (Cα rmsds 0.2–0.3 Å).
evidence: Experimental data from this study

claim: The N-terminal helices of hRio2NES-R and CPEB4NES-R that span Φ0–Φ3 bind CRM1 much like the helix of the plus direction PKINES.
source: The N-terminal helices of hRio2NES-R and CPEB4NES-R that span Φ0–Φ3 bind CRM1 much like the helix of the plus direction PKINES.
evidence: Experimental data from this study

claim: Smaller hydrophobic residues such as leucine in the Φ3 position and isoleucine, leucine, and valine in the Φ4 position of hRio2NES-R are preferred for binding to CRM1.
source: Pull-down assays with single amino acid mutants of hRio2NES-R reveal that smaller hydrophobic residues such as leucine in the Φ3 position and isoleucine, leucine, and valine in the Φ4 position are preferred for binding to CRM1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 5C

claim: When the sequence and the hydrophobic spacing pattern of an NES are reversed, the direction of the peptide binding CRM1 is also reversed.
source: The structures of CRM1-bound hRio2NES-R and CPEB4NES-R peptides support the idea that the spacing between the hydrophobic residues is critical for determining the orientation the NES binds. When the sequence and the hydrophobic spacing pattern of an NES are reversed, the direction of the peptide binding CRM1 is also reversed.
evidence: Inference based on structural data from this study

claim: Binding affinities of the NESs are similar regardless of binding orientation.
source: However, binding affinities of the NESs are similar regardless of binding orientation, consistent with the observation that hydrophobic interactions between the CRM1 groove and side chains in the Φ positions of hRio2NES and CPEB4NES, which likely govern CRM1-NES affinity, are preserved in hRio2NES-R and CPEB4NES-R.
evidence: Experimental data from binding affinity measurements and inference

claim: PKINES-Flip1 does not interact with CRM1 in pull-down assays.
source: PKINES-Flip1 does not interact with CRM1 in pull-down assays, while PKINES-Flip2 and PKINES-Flip3 show graded increases in CRM1 binding (Figure 6B).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 6B

claim: PKINES-Flip2 and PKINES-Flip3 show graded increases in CRM1 binding.
source: PKINES-Flip1 does not interact with CRM1 in pull-down assays, while PKINES-Flip2 and PKINES-Flip3 show graded increases in CRM1 binding (Figure 6B).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down assays shown in Figure 6B

claim: The structure of PKINES-Flip3 bound to CRM1 was solved at 2.5 Å resolution.
source: We solved the structure of PKINES-Flip3 bound to CRM1 at 2.5 Å resolution and it indeed binds in the minus direction (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: Experimental data from this study shown in Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Table 1

claim: PKINES-Flip3 binds in the minus direction.
source: We solved the structure of PKINES-Flip3 bound to CRM1 at 2.5 Å resolution and it indeed binds in the minus direction (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: Experimental data from this study shown in Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Table 1

claim: NES binding in the minus vs plus direction is determined by placement of the ΦXΦ pattern at the N- or C-terminal end of the NES peptide.
source: These results show that NES binding in the minus vs plus direction is determined by placement of the ΦXΦ pattern at the N- or C-terminal end of the NES peptide.
evidence: Inference based on structural and mutagenesis data from this study

claim: Hydrophobic side chains of the N-terminal ΦXΦ segment of a minus NES should be long enough to reach into binding pockets and pack with the CRM1 groove favorably.
source: Secondary to this positioning, hydrophobic side chains of the N-terminal ΦXΦ segment of a minus NES should be long enough to reach into binding pockets and pack with the CRM1 groove favorably.
evidence: Inference based on structural and mutagenesis data from this study

claim: The discovery that CRM1 binds NESs in both the plus and minus directions almost doubles the number of possible NES consensus sequences.
source: The discovery that CRM1 binds NESs in both the plus and minus directions almost doubles the number of possible NES consensus sequences.
evidence: Inference based on the discovery of bidirectional binding

claim: Each of the asymmetric class 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d patterns could be reversed to give class 1a-R, 1b-R, 1c-R, and 1d-R patterns that represent minus NESs.
source: Of the six NES patterns in Figure 1A, class 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d patterns are asymmetric, whereas class 2 and class 3 patterns are symmetric. Each of the asymmetric class 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d patterns, which represent plus NESs, could be reversed to give class 1a-R, 1b-R, 1c-R, and 1d-R patterns that represent minus NESs (Figure 7A).
evidence: Inference based on the discovery of bidirectional binding, shown in Figure 7A

claim: Matches for both class 1 (plus) and class 1-R (minus) patterns appear to be similarly prevalent in the 246 CRM1 cargos in the Dbase dataset (1849 minus vs 1950 plus matches).
source: Matches for both class 1 (plus) and class 1-R (minus) patterns appear to be similarly prevalent in the 246 CRM1 cargos (1849 minus vs 1950 plus matches) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Bioinformatic analysis of the Dbase dataset shown in Figure 7B

claim: Plus patterns seem to be somewhat enriched within NES regions (340 plus vs 230 minus matches; Chi-square test, p-value = 1.378e−05).
source: However, plus patterns seem to be somewhat enriched within NES regions (340 plus vs 230 minus matches; Chi-square test, p-value = 1.378e−05) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Bioinformatic analysis of the Dbase dataset shown in Figure 7B

claim: The bias for plus patterns in previously reported NES regions may be a consequence of NES searches that were guided solely by the plus consensus patterns.
source: The bias for plus patterns in these previously reported NES regions may be a consequence of NES searches that were guided solely by the plus consensus patterns, since the minus patterns were unknown.
evidence: Speculation based on the historical lack of knowledge about minus patterns

claim: Only 60% of previously reported class 1 NESs that were tested recently were found to actually bind CRM1.
source: The Dbase data set is further complicated by a lack of validation of direct CRM1-NES interactions. Only 60% of previously reported class 1 NESs that were tested recently were found to actually bind CRM1 (Xu et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Xu et al., 2012a)

claim: 40% (116) of the 290 NES regions in Dbase contain sequences that match both class 1 (plus) and class 1-R (minus) patterns.
source: Of the 290 NES regions in Dbase, 40% (116) contain sequences that match both class 1 (plus) and class 1-R (minus) patterns (Figure 7C).
evidence: Bioinformatic analysis of the Dbase dataset shown in Figure 7C

claim: 89 NES regions match class 1 pattern exclusively and 24 match class 1-R patterns exclusively.
